title: The magi (Matthew 2:1–12)
hook: stargazers from the east follow a light and kneel before a toddler

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon and Anna, two people who had waited, and knew the child when he came. Your line was waiting is not wasted. Who did you honor? Today a new stretch of the road begins, the road through Galilee. Day forty-four.

Jerusalem, a king's court, and visitors nobody expected. Matthew says they came from the east: men who read the night sky for meaning. Somewhere far away they saw something they couldn't ignore, and they set out. Matthew doesn't say how long the road was, or how many walked it. He says only that they came, and that in the capital they asked a dangerous question out loud. In the King James Bible: "Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him." The king on the throne is Herod. Today, the magi.
screen: `A KING'S COURT, AND VISITORS.` → `A STAR IN THE EAST.` → `WHERE IS HE THAT IS BORN KING?`

segments.voice: Matthew calls them magoi, and he never says how many there were. Three is a guess, made later, from the three gifts. He never calls them kings either; that came later too, from psalms about kings bringing gifts. And their names, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, come from later legend. What the word magoi meant was something like wise men or astrologers: learned stargazers, perhaps from Persia or Babylon, though Matthew says only the east, and outsiders to Israel's faith. Herod is troubled, Matthew says, and all Jerusalem with him. The chief priests and scribes look it up: the prophet Micah points to Bethlehem. Herod sends the visitors on, and asks them to come back and tell him where the child is, so that he can worship too. He doesn't mean it. They go, and the star goes before them, and when it stops, the King James says, "they rejoiced with exceeding great joy." Exceeding great joy. Matthew piles up the words. They find the child with Mary his mother, in a house, Matthew says, and they kneel. Then they open their treasures: "gold, and frankincense, and myrrh." An old Christian reading takes the gifts as gold for a king, incense for God, myrrh for a death to come. Then, warned in a dream, they go home another way. And notice: the first people in Matthew's Gospel to worship Jesus are foreigners, following the light they had, a star, not a scripture. Western churches remember them at Epiphany, the feast of the light shown to the nations.
screen: `NO NUMBER, NO CROWNS, NO NAMES.` · `STARGAZERS FROM THE EAST.` · `GOLD, FRANKINCENSE AND MYRRH.` · `HOME ANOTHER WAY.` · then, large: `THEY REJOICED WITH EXCEEDING GREAT JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Now ask: what has been pulling at my attention lately? Not a duty. A curiosity. A question you keep coming back to, a book you keep meaning to open, a person you'd like to know better, a place you keep wondering about. Don't judge whether it's important. The magi followed a light in the sky. Just find yours and look at it for a while. If you pray, you can ask where it leads. The bell holds the time.
The magi. Stargazers from the east, no number given, who followed a light and knelt before a child. Our word magic comes from the same root.
Your line: follow the star you have. Today, follow one small curiosity, just one step further than you normally would. Day forty-four.

howItsDone: Western churches celebrate the magi at Epiphany on January 6, and in many countries children mark it with processions, sweets or chalked blessings over doorways. In Orthodox churches January 6 centers on the baptism of Jesus, and the magi are remembered at Christmas.

original.note: Greek: magi, learned stargazers, perhaps from Persia or Babylon. Magic comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: three kings on camels in a Christmas card.
what it means: an unnumbered group of foreign stargazers who followed the light they had and knelt before a child.
what a scholar hears: magoi was a word for a Persian priestly class and for astrologers, and the kings, the number three and the names all came from later tradition, not from Matthew.

notes: Opens the part 'The road through Galilee' (weeks 7–8, days 44–56).

The magi as kings is traced to readings of Psalm 72:10–11 and Isaiah 60; the number three to the three gifts; the names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar to later Western tradition (around the sixth century). Confirm the phrasing 'centuries after'.

The symbolic reading of the gifts (gold for a king, incense for God, myrrh for death) goes back at least to early church writers such as Irenaeus; stated as a long-standing reading, not as the text's meaning.
'Magic' derives from the same root (Greek magos via Latin); confirm.
Epiphany: Western churches center January 6 on the magi; Orthodox churches keep it as Theophany, the baptism of Jesus. Churches on the Julian calendar keep these dates thirteen days later.
'Home another way' paraphrases Matthew 2:12 ('departed into their own country another way').
